placement.adaptiveSays: Adaptive: a few questions per tower. {streak} right answers in a row credit the tower and open what builds on it; {errors} mistakes in one tower end it for this check.
placement.targetSays: Up to a level: each tower is asked like a real conquest of the chosen level — all its cards; conquered, you move on.
placement.doneBefore: This check has run already — again, it asks only what is still open.
placement.skippedBefore: Last time you went on without checking.
placement.endTitle: Done — this is how much you already know
placement.nothingCredited: No tower was credited this time.
placement.recommended: Recommended: first check how much you already know
placement.placed: credited by placement — cards still to be confirmed
placement.why: Why check? If you already know something, you do not have to walk the whole way to it. Every tower you pass here counts at once and opens the ways that build on it — so you get to what is new for you much faster. Nothing is lost if you do not know something: you simply learn it later on the way.
placement.adaptivePros: quick — a few questions per tower, many towers in a short time; it goes on to what builds on what you know.
placement.adaptiveCons: a credited tower (◇) is an estimate, not a conquest at a level; its cards you were not asked come later in reviews.
placement.targetPros: a tower passed here is really conquered at that level and counts like any conquest — nothing to do again.
placement.targetCons: slower — every card of each tower is asked, so it fits best when you know a part of the course well.
placement.levelSays: The level is how well you must know a tower: level 1 is the lightest (most answers right), higher levels need more right answers, at the first try. A higher level takes longer, but the tower then stands higher at once.

welcome.title: The knowledge map
welcome.text: Knowledge is not a list of chapters but a landscape: topics depend on each other, and to understand one you need others. This map shows those dependencies. So at any moment you can see what you already know, what you can start now and how far it is to your goal. The guide walks you through your own map: you click what it shows, then read what it is and why it works this way.

home.title: Start
home.do: Click the house — the pulsing spot on the map.
home.text: The house is the starting point. Stories leaving it assume nothing — you can begin with them without any knowledge. The house is also where you come back. From here you review everything you have seen at once (you choose how well known something may be and still be skipped), see the ways that bring something new, and open this guide again.

tower.title: Tower = topic
tower.text: A tower is one topic: a dozen or so questions that together check whether you understand it. The colour is the field. The height is how many cards stand between you and conquering the tower — including the towers it requires — so it honestly shows how much work is ahead. A pale tower is a topic nothing of which has come up yet. With every card you learn, it gains colour and shrinks. Once clicked, only the buttons that make sense right now stand above it.

path.title: Path = story
path.do: Click the highlighted path (or its marker).
path.text: A path is a story: slides and questions that explain the topic before it is checked. Towers and paths are separate on purpose. The tower says WHAT you need to know; the path says HOW you can learn it. Several stories can lead to one tower, and one story can introduce cards of several towers, so the same knowledge can be reached in different ways. A solid line means you can go. Dashed with a lock: the story assumes knowledge you do not have yet. The arrow shows the direction, and on a chosen path the dots are slides (●) and questions (◆).

started.title: On the way
started.text: This is a story half done: the path is coloured up to the last slide seen, and the tower has gained colour and shrunk by the cards that already came up. You can stop anywhere — the map remembers where you left off, and you come back from there.

level.title: Conquering
level.text: Having seen the cards is not the same as mastering the topic. That is why a tower is conquered in a run: each card once, in random order, without the story's explanations. Each of the {levels} levels asks more and lights another arc on top of the tower. You do not need the highest level to go on: the ways out of a tower open from the level the course author set, and higher levels only show how firmly the topic sits. The star (everything right the first time) is not a requirement either — it is a distinction that shows what else can be achieved.

conquered.title: Conquered
conquered.text: A conquered tower is flat: there is nothing left to learn in it, so it does not hide the topics further on. The flag marks the conquest, the star a run without a single mistake the first time. The dot in the middle says how fresh the knowledge is: green — fresh, yellow — review soon. Only a conquered tower opens the ways that build on it, because the next topics assume this one is mastered.
conquered.text0: When you know all its cards, the tower is conquered and flat: there is nothing left to learn in it, so it does not hide the topics further on. The dot in the middle says how fresh the knowledge is: green — fresh, yellow — review soon, orange — time to review (then "Review" stands above the tower). Only a conquered tower opens the ways that build on it.

due.title: Due for review
due.text: Memory fades over time — that is normal, not a failure. A review helps most just when knowledge starts to blur: then the dot turns orange and "Review" appears above the tower. Each good review lengthens the time to the next. Only conquered towers are reviewed, so reviews do not flood topics still being learned. One more thing: when you choose a longer way and there are cards along it that the system thinks may have faded, the way starts with a short review of them — before building something new on them, you check whether you still remember them.

onward.title: Ways on
onward.text: Above a conquered tower stand the ways that leave it and bring something new — new cards or a tower still missing. Ways already travelled or bringing nothing are left out, so the choice stays simple. Pointing at a way lights it on the map. When something is due, "Review" stands next to them, coloured by how much it is needed.

locked.title: A tower that waits
locked.do: Click the tall tower standing on discs.
locked.text: This tower requires other topics. The discs under it are the towers still missing — the bottom one comes first. Requirements are not there for their own sake: this tower's questions assume that knowledge, and without it they would be guesswork. "Explore" lays out the shortest way through the missing topics and guides you step by step. "Conquer directly" lets you try without that way — if you already know it from elsewhere, you do not have to prove it twice.

fork.title: Fork
fork.text: Here the story splits: the branches tell the same thing differently or lead to different topics. You choose one; you can come back to the others later — nothing is lost.

sign.title: Signpost
sign.text: A signpost is a question answered by several steps of the map at once, for example "Who was…?". It stands where that way begins. Clicking it guides you through all the stories and towers needed, in order, and at the end you can check whether the answer is clear now.

way.title: Guidance
way.do: Click the tall tower again, then “Explore” above it.
way.text: “Explore” (or a double click on a tower) chooses the tower as your goal and turns on guidance. Now you see the whole way to it: the bright paths are what is still ahead, the arcs in the air show which topics it needs, and the camera shows the whole map so nothing of the way is hidden. At the bottom the same way appears as a bar of steps; each step says what will happen and gives a choice — go, skip, or restore a skipped one. Skipping is allowed on purpose: sometimes you want to get to a particular place straight away and fill in the rest later. A double click on empty ground ends the guidance; the progress stays.

views.title: Views
views.text: At the top, views narrow the map: what I know, to discover (what you can start now), to review, gaps. "Check what you know" asks the key questions of every topic and shows the gaps — a good start if you already know something. Open this guide again by clicking the house.

steps.title: Steps of a way
steps.do: Click one of the steps in the bar at the bottom.
steps.text: Every way is laid out in steps: a story (reading the slides), learning (cards no story brings), a review, and conquering a tower. "Go to step" stands above the current step. A clicked step shows on the map where it lies and gives a choice: "Go here" starts it at once, even before earlier ones, and "Skip" greys it out — it stays in its place and can be restored with the same click ("Restore"). Try it in the bar: skip a step and restore it. "≡" shows the whole way with its forks, and "End" stops the way without losing progress.

placement.title: Checking what you already know
placement.do: Click the tower with the dashed ring.
placement.text: Not everyone starts from zero. The check ("Check how much you already know", at the start of a course or a story) asks real questions from the towers that can be passed right now — on the map they are in colour, the rest grey. A tower passed this way has a dashed ring: it counts as passable, opens everything built on it, and its cards that were not asked come later in reviews. There are two ways. Adaptive: a few questions per tower — a few right answers in a row pass it, a few mistakes end it; quick and many towers at once, but an estimate. Up to a level: each tower is asked like a real conquest of the chosen level — slower, but the tower is truly conquered and nothing needs redoing.

arcs.title: Arcs in the air
arcs.text: The grey arcs above the map are not ways but dependencies: they show where the knowledge comes from that this tower needs, or that is needed to enter a path. An arc runs from the tower you must know to the tower (or the gate on a path) that requires it; the arrow at its end shows the direction. A dashed arc means this knowledge is still missing; a solid one that the requirement is met. The arcs are in the air on purpose: you walk on the ground (the paths), and in the air you only see what you must know beforehand. They appear when you click a tower or a fork, or choose a goal.

full.title: Conquer fully: {name}
full.says: This tower is already conquered and opens the ways on — higher levels and the star are not needed for that. They only show how firmly the topic sits. Each run asks every card once, in random order.
full.star: Masterly — every card right the first time (all levels at once)
full.how: A run raises you by every level whose rule it meets. One mistake does not undo your learning: every answer counts for your knowledge.
